newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW--Minn Fed's Rolnick wary of money growth.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW--Minn Fed's Rolnick wary of money growth.

text.p: U.S. short-term monetary aggregates are a little above the Federal Reserve's targets, an1 indication the central bank should be careful with how much money it pumps into the economy, a top official at the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis said.
"Right now the short-term monetary aggregates are a little above our targets, the Fed targets," Arthur Rolnick, director of research at the Minneapolis Fed, told Reuters.

"It's a red flag; I don't think we're in a danger zone necessarily, but I think it's something we have to watch carefully, that we don't put too much money into the economy and then the money supply grow too fast," he added.

The Minneapolis director of research added, however, that in the long-run, the "five-year moving average is what we've been looking at at the Fed. It seems to be a pretty good indicator of where inflation goes."
Rolnick said the U.S. economy is currently moving at a brisk pace, adding that he expects it to remain like that as long as inflation stays low.
"The economy is probably doing the best it has ever done. In terms of employment gains, in terms of output, in terms of opportunities, in terms of the future outlook, this economy is really strong.
"... And it should continue to do well assuming we may maintain a low-inflation environment," the economist said.
Asked about his assessment of current levels of consumer spending, Rolnick said some indicators might suggest Americans are spending less. But he indicated the underlying trend remains firm.

"You might see some indicators that suggest consumers aren't spending or that business isn't investing or that there is concern about consumer debt ... But despite those concerns, consumers have been spending and the economy has done real well over the last year," he said.
"I think this economy is poised for long-term, sustainable growth," he added.

Rolnick said labor markets were healthy. He also said he expected productivity to pick-up, which would be followed by a rise in real wages. The economist said such a phenomena, if confirmed, should be seen as a sign of a health economy.

"I do expect some pick-up in productivity, which means some pick-up in real wages and that's terrific ... There's nothing wrong with that. That doesn't portend more inflation, that portends a healthy economy," he said.
The head of research at the Minneapolis Fed shunned some theories that argue the Non-Accelerating Inflation Rate of Unemployment (NAIRU) was a faithful measure of future inflation.
"I can speak about literature that I've read, and literature says that the NAIRU is not a very good predictor of (long-term) inflation," he said.
Rolnick also said he was optimistic about the international economic scenario.

"World trade is booming. Trade is what economies are all about. The more trade you get, the stronger economies are going to get. So, my views tend to be pretty optimistic when I look how world economies are going," he said.
He said several countries, such as China, Russia and the former Soviet Republics, India and South Africa, were opening their economies, adding that U.S. firms should benefit from that.
"Many of these economies are opening up their economies to new technology, new trade. They need the infrastructure. Our companies are poised to deliver much of that," he said.
